glossary.Milani: ESA's 12 kg CubeSat, released by the Hera mission at the asteroid Didymos and its moon Dimorphos. Its body is a 13 x 25 x 37 cm box with two solar panels that fold out to 1.47 m across. It may land on Dimorphos at the end of its mission; these simulations ask how it would bounce.
glossary.panels open / folded: The craft's two shapes in the simulations, both 12 kg. Panels open: the body with both solar panels unfolded, 1.47 m across. Panels folded: the body alone, 37 cm long. (The code calls them deployed and stowed.)
glossary.Dimorphos: The 150 m moon of the asteroid Didymos, hit by NASA's DART spacecraft in 2022. Its surface is a pile of boulders, with smaller stones and finer material between and on them.
glossary.Dimorphos gravity: 5e-5 m/s^2, 200 000 times weaker than Earth's, used in every drop. A craft leaving the surface at 1 cm/s rises for 200 s before it falls back. (Also written micro-g.)
glossary.LMGC90: The open-source contact-dynamics code (University of Montpellier) that simulates every grain and the craft as rigid bodies colliding with friction, run through its Python interface (pylmgc90).
glossary.contact dynamics (NSCD): LMGC90's method: rigid bodies whose collisions are solved as impulses within each time step, not as springs, which allows long time steps (5 ms in drops, 2 ms while settling). NSCD stands for non-smooth contact dynamics.
glossary.contact solver (NLGS): The part of LMGC90 that finds every contact force in a time step. It sweeps over the contacts until the forces stop changing (to a tolerance) or a budget of 10 000 sweeps runs out; a step that uses the whole budget is 'unconverged'. NLGS stands for non-linear Gauss-Seidel.
glossary.grain: One boulder or small stone. Every grain is a random convex polyhedron (a solid with flat faces): 12 corners for boulders, 10 for small stones, about 1 : 0.7 : 0.5 in length : width : thickness, flat and angular like the boulders DART imaged.
glossary.grain size: Sizes on these pages are lengths: a grain's longest dimension. The bed files give half of it (r_min_m and r_max_m, the 'long semi-axis'). Measured on the settled beds, real grains come out about 10 % shorter than twice r, because only 10-12 corners outline each one.
glossary.contact rule: How LMGC90 treats two touching bodies; every rule includes friction. Position rule (GAP_SGR_CLB): at the end of each step no two bodies may overlap, and an overlap is pushed out; nothing bounces. Speed rule (RST_CLB): bodies stop moving into each other and bounce back with a set fraction of their approach speed (none while settling, half in drops); an overlap that already exists stays.
glossary.split contact rule: How beds with small stones are settled: the position rule between boulders and between a boulder and a small stone (so boulders do not sink into the stones), the speed rule between two small stones (with the position rule there they never come to rest on the boulders). Used since 30 October.
glossary.friction: Friction coefficient 0.6 between grains (a grain slides on a slope steeper than 31 degrees) and 0.5 between the craft and a grain. Settling uses the same 0.6: higher friction made the contact solver fail (1 November).
glossary.bed: Simulated ground: grains poured into a square box, left to settle under Earth's gravity, saved once, and reused by every drop on it. A bed's size is the side of its box: 4.5 m x 4.5 m for the study beds, 2-4 m for laptop tests.
glossary.boulders: Grains 20-70 cm long (30-70 cm in study bed 1). Boulders of this size cover most of Dimorphos.
glossary.small stones: Grains 8-16 cm long (10-20 cm in study bed 5's bottom layer). They stand in for the smaller material between and on Dimorphos's boulders. They are not fine-grained: sand or gravel would take millions of grains per square metre, far beyond what can be simulated, so no bed has fine-grained material. (The code calls them fines.)
glossary.thin top layer: Small stones poured on the boulders, enough for an 8 cm layer (study beds 4 and 5). The stones are 5-10 cm thick, so the layer is about one stone deep and the tops of the boulders stick out through it. (The code calls it the veneer.)
glossary.thick top layer: 25 cm of small stones on the boulders (study bed 6).
glossary.bottom layer: 30 cm of small stones under the boulders (study bed 5): boulders resting on loose stones instead of on the box's rigid floor. (The code calls it the substrate.)
glossary.even size mix: Every length between the smallest and the largest is equally likely (study bed 1: 30-70 cm). (The code calls it uniform.)
glossary.realistic size mix: Many small boulders and few large ones, in the proportions measured on DART's images of Dimorphos: the share of boulders longer than D falls like exp(-(D / 0.033 m)^0.39), a Weibull distribution (Pajola et al. 2024, fitted to boulders 1-16 m long). The beds keep only 20-70 cm, so most boulders are near 20 cm and a few are large. Study beds 2-6. (The code calls it weibull.)
glossary.settle: Letting poured grains fall and stop. Beds are settled under Earth's gravity (9.81 m/s^2): a pile stops within seconds of simulated time instead of hours, and the drops then run at Dimorphos gravity. A bed is settled when it is at rest and still at rest after the 500-step check.
glossary.at rest: How a settle decides the grains have stopped: over the last simulated second the median grain moved less than 3 mm, 95 % moved less than 6 cm, none more than 30 cm. Piles of angular grains never stop jiggling completely, so 'at rest' means the pile's shape no longer changes.
glossary.speed limit: While settling no grain may move faster than 0.3 m/s; without it piles blow apart.
glossary.500-step check: After a bed first comes to rest, 500 more steps with nothing changed; the bed must still be at rest at the end. If it blows apart instead, the state saved at the first rest is the bed, with a warning.
glossary.layers of a bed: A bed is poured in layers (boulders, then small stones), each settled before the next. A finished layer is reused by every bed that starts with the same layers. (The code calls them stages.)
glossary.quality checks (QA): Automatic checks on every bed and drop, graded PASS, WARN (look at it) or FAIL (not used). Beds: overlaps, escaped grains, contacts per grain, layer height. Drops: how it ended, that the first touch was on a grain that can move, no energy created, grain motion at the patch edge, the solver.
glossary.study beds 1-6: The six beds of the study, each one change from the one before; all 4.5 m x 4.5 m with 0.9 m of boulders unless stated, settled on the lab Mac. 1: boulders, even size mix (30-70 cm). 2: boulders, realistic size mix (20-70 cm). 3: bed 2, 1.5 m deep. 4: bed 2 plus a thin top layer of small stones. 5: a bottom layer of small stones, then bed 4. 6: bed 2 plus a thick top layer of small stones.
glossary.laptop test beds: Smaller or copied beds settled on the laptop to try things quickly: bed 1 itself (the same bed as the lab Mac's); bed 1's recipe at 4 m x 4 m; bed 2's boulders at 3 m x 3 m; 20-50 cm boulders, 0.5 m deep, with a thin top layer, at 2 m x 2 m; bed 1's boulders with a thin top layer at 3 m x 3 m.
glossary.bed size: The side of a bed's box. A drop needs the patch plus 0.75 m on every side kept away from the walls (the largest boulder, 70 cm, plus 5 cm), where grains packed against the walls: side = 2 x (patch radius + 0.75 m) + the spread of the landing spots. With the panels open (1.2 m patch) that is at least 3.9 m; with them folded (0.7 m patch), 2.9 m.
glossary.drop: One simulated landing of the craft on one spot of one settled bed, from just before the first touch until the bounce is over. (The code calls it a run.)
glossary.drop set: Drops run together from one file. (The code calls it a campaign.)
glossary.36-drop set: The same 36 landings on every study bed: 9 landing spots (a 3 x 3 grid 30 cm apart) x 2 arrival speeds (4 and 8 cm/s) x 2 angles (0 and 40 degrees from vertical), the craft always in the same pose.
glossary.start conditions: What is set before a drop: the bed, the landing spot, the arrival speed, the angle from vertical, the approach direction, the craft's shape and its pose.
glossary.landing spot: Where the craft is aimed, in metres from the bed's centre (x, y).
glossary.angle from vertical: 0 degrees: straight down. 40 degrees: arriving obliquely, moving sideways at 64 % of its speed.
glossary.approach direction: The compass direction the craft comes from, in degrees from the bed's +x axis. (The code calls it the azimuth.)
glossary.patch: A drop does not simulate the whole bed: only grains in a circle around the landing spot can move. That circle is the patch: radius 1.2 m with the panels open, 0.7 m with them folded on 3 m beds. (The code calls it the crop.)
glossary.fixed ring: The grains just outside the patch that touch it, held still so the patch keeps its support. The craft can hit them; they do not move. (The code calls them frozen.)
glossary.rest of the bed: Everything beyond the fixed ring: left out of the drop, and treated as fixed ground by the checks made after it.
glossary.reach: The largest distance from the craft's centre of mass to any point of the craft: 0.76 m with the panels open, 0.23 m folded. Whatever the craft's rotation, all of it lies within this distance.
glossary.touch: One period of contact between the craft and the ground, from the step the solver first puts a force on the craft to the step the force is gone. A drop can have several: the craft tips onto a panel, rocks, skips.
glossary.speed ratio e: Exit speed divided by arrival speed. 0: the craft stopped; 1: it left as fast as it came. The main bounce number.
glossary.restitution: The share of the velocity across a surface that survives a bounce (normal restitution), or along it (tangential).
glossary.energy kept: The craft's energy when it left, divided by its energy on arrival (motion plus spin, height counted from the first touch).
glossary.how a drop ends: Bounced off: left the ground, and its exact free flight comes back down on none of the grains the drop can move. Left the patch: slid or hopped out of the patch while on the ground, so the result is cut off. Captured: stayed down, creeping. Came to rest. Ran out of time: 300 s simulated.
glossary.free flight: The craft between touches or after its last one. Only gravity acts on it, and gravity cannot make it turn faster or slower, so its path and its tumbling can be computed exactly.
glossary.next touch: Where and when the craft would touch the bed again after a drop has ended, from its exact free flight. 'Off the patch': on the fixed ring or the rest of the bed, the landing of a new hop.
glossary.convex: A shape without dents: the straight line between any two of its points stays inside it. Every grain and every piece of the craft is convex, which makes the exact distance between two of them a small, reliable calculation.
glossary.ballast: A massless box inside the craft's body (panels open). LMGC90 turns a body made of several pieces about the centre of their volumes, not of their masses; the ballast's volume moves that point onto the craft's true centre of mass.
glossary.centre of mass: The point a free body turns about and whose path is a ballistic arc. With the panels open it lies 6 mm from the centre of the craft's body, toward the panels.
glossary.conservative advancement: Moving a body forward in steps no longer than its distance to the nearest obstacle divided by the speed of its fastest point, so it cannot pass through anything between two tests.
glossary.replay: Running a drop again from its saved setup. The simulation is deterministic, so the replay matches step for step (94 of 94 checked); movies and checks are made this way after the fact.
glossary.ParaView: The open-source 3-D viewer. LMGC90 writes frames for it (every 0.1 s for the first 15 s of a drop, then every second); the movies are rendered by ParaView itself.
glossary.lab Mac: The 24-core Mac Studio in the lab that settles the study beds and runs their drop sets. The laptop runs small tests and the analyses on these pages.

methods.name: The craft model
methods.definition: Milani is rigid convex boxes: a 13 x 24.6 x 36.6 cm body of 10.8 kg and, with the panels open, two solar panels 1 cm thick and 59 x 36.6 cm, 0.6 kg each: 12 kg in all. With the panels folded it is the body alone at 12 kg. Mass, centre of mass and inertia come from the pieces' own masses. Inside the body (panels open) sits a massless ballast box (3.9 x 24 x 36 cm, 3 mm inside every wall): LMGC90 places a body made of several pieces at the centre of their volumes rather than of their masses (mod_RBDY3, reading the bodies), and the ballast's volume moves that point onto the centre of mass.
methods.why: Without it the craft with open panels turned about a point 10.2 mm from its centre of mass: the panels are far lighter for their volume than the body. Found on 1 November by comparing the craft in the simulation's own frames with its design. Every drop now checks that the simulated craft sits within 0.1 mm of its design (it does, to 1e-11 m). No grain can reach the ballast without pushing 3 mm into the body first.
methods.caveat: Drops made before 1 November have the 10 mm offset: the laptop's were re-simulated on 1 November, the lab Mac's weekend drops still need it (lab.py campaign rerun --stale). On one 4 m bed drop the fix moved e from 0.300 to 0.329; with the panels folded the craft is one piece and was never affected.

code.excerpt:
def ballast_piece(pcs, inset: float = BALLAST_INSET_M):
    """An internal box that puts the craft's VOLUME centroid on its centre of
    mass. LMGC90 places a multi-contactor body's centre at the volume-weighted
    centroid of its contactors' geometric volumes (mod_RBDY3, read_bodies:
    OG = sum(v_i shift_i) / sum(v_i)) and keeps the principal inertia it is
    given, so a craft whose pieces differ in density (deployed: bus 10.8 kg,
    wings 0.6 kg each) turned about a point 10.2 mm from its centre of mass
    until 2026-11-01. The ballast lies `inset` inside the bus on every side,
    so no grain can reach it before the bus; None when the volumes already
    balance (one piece, or uniform density)."""
    M = sum(p.mass for p in pcs)
    com = sum(p.mass * p.centre for p in pcs) / M
    S = sum(float(np.prod(p.dims)) * (p.centre - com) for p in pcs)
    if float(np.linalg.norm(S)) < 1e-12:
        return None
    bus = next(p for p in pcs if p.name == "bus")
    if not np.allclose(bus.axes, np.eye(3)):
        raise NotImplementedError("ballast: the bus must be aligned with the bus frame")
    k = int(np.argmax(np.abs(S)))
    if float(np.abs(np.delete(S, k)).max()) > 1e-9 * abs(float(S[k])):
        raise NotImplementedError(f"ballast: volume imbalance off the bus axes {S}")
    h = 0.5 * np.asarray(bus.dims, dtype=float) - inset
    side = -float(np.sign(S[k]))                  # the ballast sits opposite the imbalance
    face = float(bus.centre[k]) + side * h[k]     # inner face of the bus wall on that side
    A = float(np.prod(np.delete(2.0 * h, k)))
    a = side * (face - float(com[k]))             # from the centre of mass to that face, > 0
    need = abs(float(S[k])) / A                   # the ballast's length L solves L (a - L/2) = need
    disc = a * a - 2.0 * need
    if disc < 0:
        raise ValueError("ballast: the bus cannot hold enough volume to centre the craft")
    L = a - math.sqrt(disc)
    dims = 2.0 * h
    dims[k] = L
    centre = np.asarray(bus.centre, dtype=float).copy()
    centre[k] = face - side * 0.5 * L
    return _box_piece("ballast", 0.0, tuple(dims), centre, np.eye(3))

methods.name: In contact (a touch)
methods.definition: At each 5 ms time step the craft is in contact when the resultant contact force the solver applied to it is non-zero: |R| > 1e-12 N.
methods.why: This is the solver's own statement that some contact transmitted force in that step. Bodies that are merely close (within the detection distance) carry zero force and do not count. Non-smooth contact dynamics resolves even an instantaneous collision as an impulse inside its time step, and contact detection looks 15 mm ahead (the alert distance) while the craft moves at most 0.4 mm per step at 8 cm/s, so no touch can fall between two steps.
methods.caveat: A resultant can in principle cancel when the craft is squeezed equally from opposite sides; the contact count column of the trajectory (n_box_contacts) would show such a case, and none has been seen.

methods.name: First contact and arrival velocity
methods.definition: The first step in contact. The arrival velocity is the craft's velocity one step before it, the last free-flight state.
methods.why: Taking the state before the touch keeps the arrival velocity free of the impact itself.

methods.name: Touches (contact episodes)
methods.definition: How many times the craft goes from free to in contact during the drop.

methods.name: Last contact
methods.definition: The last step at which the craft was in contact before the drop ended.
methods.why: Within the simulated time this is exact (every step is tested). Whether a later touch would have come is what the end-of-drop test and the last-contact check below settle.

methods.name: Exit state (exit speed, spin, elevation)
methods.definition: The craft's velocity and spin at the step its contact ended for the last time. Each separation overwrites it, so at the end it is the last one. Exit elevation is the angle of the exit velocity above the horizontal of the bed (not of the local surface).

methods.name: Bounced off: when a drop is over
methods.definition: A drop ends as 'bounced off' when the craft has been free for 0.5 s, is rising, and its exact free flight (next entry) does not come back down on a grain the drop can move, the patch, within the time the drop could still take (up to 300 s). Until that holds the simulation goes on and the solver decides, also when the craft's centre has crossed the patch's edge but a panel is still over it. The flight is checked against the whole bed: 'clear' if it touches nothing in that time, 'beyond' if its next touch is on the fixed ring or the rest of the bed; the prediction is stored with the drop.
methods.why: Once the craft is free nothing acts on it but gravity, so its future is known exactly: nothing is left to simulate unless it comes back down on grains the drop can move. The test it replaced, a 3-30 s look-ahead of the tumbling craft, missed a panel-tip graze 19 s after a drop on bed 1 had been declared over (31 October). The exact test also ends drops sooner: a 4 m-bed drop now stops 0.5 s after its last touch instead of 31 s later, with the same result, at a seventh of the computing.
methods.caveat: The patch's grains are taken at their pose when the test is made, and a grain still moving could come into the path afterwards. The test allows for it (its 1 cm margin grows by the fastest grain's speed times the time ahead), and the replay in the last-contact check covers the rest wherever the flight passes within 5 cm of a grain that can move.

def decide(self, x, v, M_rows, w_body, C, axes, t_now: float, horizon: float,
               grain_speed: float = 0.0):
        """None: keep simulating (the craft's next touch is on a free grain,
        or its flight passes within margin + grain_speed * t of one).
        Otherwise how the drop ends: "clear" (no touch on the bed within the
        horizon) or "beyond" (the next touch is on the frozen ring or the
        bed outside the simulation). self.last holds the scan."""
        if self._cache is None or float(np.abs(C[self.free_index] - self._cache[0]).max()) > 1e-3:
            self._cache = (C[self.free_index].copy(), self.base.with_free(self.free_meshes(C, axes)))
        r = scan(self.shape, x, v, matrix_to_quat(np.asarray(M_rows).T), w_body, self.g, self._cache[1],
                 free_margin=self.margin, free_rate=float(grain_speed), max_s=max(0.0, horizon))
        r["grain_speed_m_s"] = float(f"{grain_speed:.3g}")
        r["decided_at_t"] = round(float(t_now), 4)
        r["touch_at_t"] = round(float(t_now) + r["end_s"], 4) if r["touch"] else None
        self.last = r
        if not r["touch"]:
            return "clear"
        return None if r["layer"] == "free" else "beyond"

methods.name: Exact free flight
methods.definition: From any free state the craft's motion is computed exactly: its centre of mass on the ballistic arc, its rotation from Euler's equations for a torque-free body (the spin axis wobbles because the craft's three moments of inertia differ), integrated by 4th-order Runge-Kutta in steps of at most 0.02 s. The craft is then moved along that flight over the bed in two stages. Points every 2 cm on its surface are compared with the bed's top surface (1 cm grid, each cell raised to its highest neighbour); wherever a point comes within 2 cm, the exact distance between the craft's pieces (three convex boxes with the panels open) and every grain nearby (convex polyhedra) decides. A touch is an exact distance under 1 mm. Near a grain every step is the longest in which no point of the craft could close that distance (conservative advancement), so a touch cannot fall between two tests.
methods.why: It is the physics LMGC90 itself integrates for a free body, gyroscopic torque included, so it can be checked against the simulation: over the recorded free flights of bed 1 (10-70 s each) the predicted centre stays within 0.001 mm and the orientation within 0.06 degrees of the simulation's. The exact distance is the closest pair of points of two convex hulls, a small least-squares problem; on 1000 pairs of boxes with known distances its worst error is 2e-13 m.
methods.caveat: The patch's grains are taken as they stand (the drop's last frame for the check, the current pose in the end-of-drop test). Outside the patch the bed is as settled, which is what an undisturbed bed would be.

code.excerpt:
def _deriv(q, w, I):
    """d/dt of (q body->world, w body-frame) for a torque-free rigid body."""
    I1, I2, I3 = I
    dw = np.array([(I2 - I3) * w[1] * w[2] / I1,
                   (I3 - I1) * w[2] * w[0] / I2,
                   (I1 - I2) * w[0] * w[1] / I3])
    dq = 0.5 * _qmul(q, np.array([0.0, w[0], w[1], w[2]]))
    return dq, dw

def hull_distance(A, B, w: float = 1.0e3):
    """Distance between the convex hulls of point sets A and B (0 when they
    overlap) and the closest point of each: the smallest |p - q| over convex
    combinations p of A and q of B, a non-negative least-squares problem
    with the two sum-to-one constraints as heavily weighted rows, solved by
    bounded-variable least squares (scipy's nnls fails to converge on 10-15 %
    of touching boxes; BVLS: none of 1000, worst error 2e-13 m, 0.15 ms)."""
    from scipy.optimize import lsq_linear
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    B = np.asarray(B, dtype=float)
    o = 0.5 * (A.mean(axis=0) + B.mean(axis=0))
    a, b = (A - o).T, (B - o).T
    n, m = a.shape[1], b.shape[1]
    M = np.zeros((5, n + m))
    M[:3, :n], M[:3, n:] = a, -b
    M[3, :n], M[4, n:] = w, w
    x = lsq_linear(M, np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, w, w]), bounds=(0.0, np.inf), method="bvls", tol=1e-14).x
    p = a @ (x[:n] / x[:n].sum()) + o
    q = b @ (x[n:] / x[n:].sum()) + o
    return float(np.linalg.norm(p - q)), p, q

methods.name: Last-contact check
methods.definition: Every bounced-off drop is checked after it has finished, two ways. First, the exact free flight from its last touch over the whole bed: until the run's end against the grains outside the simulation (inside it the solver has already decided), after it against the patch's grains at their final pose, the fixed ring and the rest of the bed, until the craft has left the bed. Second, where that flight passes within 5 cm of a grain that can move, a replay of the drop with the end-of-drop test switched off, continued until the craft leaves the patch, stops, or 10-150 s past the original end. The replay is deterministic, so up to the original end it is the original run, and it includes the grains' own motion.
methods.why: Verdicts: last contact confirmed (no touch anywhere on the bed after the last touch); next touch off the patch (no later touch on the patch; the next one, shown with when and where, is the landing of a new hop on the fixed ring or the rest of the bed); touched the fixed ring as predicted (the replay runs into the touch the flight predicted there); lands back on the patch (a long hop back onto it after the drop's 300 s limit); touched again (a touch the drop should have simulated: it ended too early). On the 3 m set, replaying every drop gave the same verdicts as replaying only those within 5 cm of a grain that can move (1 November).
methods.caveat: Drops checked before 1 November had only the replay, which cannot follow a craft out over the patch's edge; they show 'left over the patch edge' until re-checked.

methods.name: Outcomes
methods.definition: bounced off: see above. left the patch: the craft's centre left the patch while on or near the ground, and its flight (if it was airborne) does not come back down on the patch (the result is cut off). came to rest: slower than 2 mm/s and 0.01 rad/s for 10 s in contact. captured: its fastest point stayed below 10 % of the arrival speed for 10 s (at micro-g friction takes minutes to stop a creep). ran out of time: 300 s simulated.

code.excerpt:
def update(self, in_contact: bool, speed: float, spin: float, rising: bool,
               ahead, left_patch: bool, point_speed: float | None = None,
               capture_speed: float | None = None, free_touch_ahead: bool = False) -> str | None:
        """Advance one step. `ahead` is a zero-argument callable, evaluated
        only when the craft has been free for detach_min_time and is rising
        (it is the expensive test): None while the craft's exact free flight
        comes back down on a free grain of the crop (keep simulating, the
        solver decides), otherwise how the drop ends: "clear" (no touch on
        the bed in the time the run could still take) or "beyond" (its next
        touch is outside the free crop) — flight.LivePredictor.
        `free_touch_ahead`: the last prediction is such a touch, still to come.

        "captured": after first contact, the box's fastest point
        (`point_speed`, e.g. v + spin x circumradius) stayed below
        `capture_speed` for rest_time without detaching. At asteroid gravity
        friction stops a creeping box only over minutes (mu g ~ 2.5e-5 m/s^2),
        so this ends runs that can no longer bounce away."""
        s = self.state
        s.t += self.dt
        if s.first_contact_t is not None and left_patch:
            if not in_contact and rising and s.free_time + self.dt >= self.detach_min_time:
                # flying out over the patch edge. Until 2026-10-31 this alone
                # ended the drop ("patch_edge"), but a wing still over the
                # crop can come down on it: b955841420ca (bed 1) touched a
                # free grain 0.58 m from the target 4 s after its run ended.
                # The exact flight decides, as anywhere else
                how = ahead()
                if how:
                    s.free_time += self.dt
                    s._in_contact = False
                    s.detached_how = how
                    return "detached"
            elif in_contact or not free_touch_ahead:
                # on the ground (sliding, rolling, hopping low) beyond the free
                # crop the box meets frozen grains or bare floor: no longer physical
                s._in_contact = in_contact
                return "left_patch"
        if in_contact:
            if s.first_contact_t is None:
                s.first_contact_t = s.t
            if not s._in_contact:
                s.episodes += 1
            s.last_contact_t = s.t
            s.free_time = 0.0
            if speed < self.rest_speed and spin < self.rest_spin:
                s.rest_time += self.dt
                if s.rest_time >= self.rest_time:
                    s._in_contact = True
                    return "rest"
            else:
                s.rest_time = 0.0
        else:
            if s.first_contact_t is None:
                s.rest_time = 0.0
                if s.t > self.contact_deadline:
                    return "no_contact"
            else:
                s.free_time += self.dt
                how = ahead() if (s.free_time >= self.detach_min_time and rising) else None
                if how:
                    s._in_contact = False

methods.name: Site slope and roughness
methods.definition: A plane fitted (least squares) to the bed's height map in a disk around the landing spot (radius: half the craft's smallest dimension, at least 0.1 m): its tilt is the slope, the RMS of heights about it the roughness.

code.excerpt:
def site(self, cx: float, cy: float, radius: float) -> dict:
        """Terrain descriptors in a disk: mean/max height, best-fit plane
        slope (deg), RMS roughness about that plane, owner ids present."""
        m = self.disk_mask(cx, cy, radius)
        if not m.any():
            raise ValueError("site disk does not overlap the height map")
        ny, nx = self.z.shape
        xs = self.x0 + self.dx * np.arange(nx)
        ys = self.y0 + self.dx * np.arange(ny)
        X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
        x, y, z = X[m], Y[m], self.z[m]
        A = np.column_stack([x - cx, y - cy, np.ones_like(x)])
        coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, z, rcond=None)
        resid = z - A @ coef
        slope = float(np.degrees(np.arctan(np.hypot(coef[0], coef[1]))))
        return {"z_mean": float(z.mean()), "z_max": float(z.max()),
                "z_center": float(self.height(cx, cy)),
                "slope_deg": slope, "roughness_rms": float(np.sqrt(np.mean(resid ** 2))),
                "owners": np.unique(self.owner[m]).tolist()}

code.excerpt:
def solver_health(postpro_dir, max_sweeps: int, first_step: int | None = None) -> dict:
    """Non-convergence is NOT an error in LMGC90 and its warning is
    suppressed by DisableLogMes (crash guide §1 gotcha 2b); the only witness
    is SOLVER_INFORMATIONS: a step whose iteration count reached the budget
    did not converge. With `first_step` (an impact's first contact, 1-based
    row) the count is also split into before and from that step on: a run
    has a fixed handful of such steps — the crop's own relaxation before
    the touch and the shock of the touch itself (8-13 per run on the 4 m
    bed, 2026-10-31) — so a fraction of ALL steps flags a 1 s run and not
    a 100 s one. The contact-phase fraction is the one to grade."""
    d = named(Path(postpro_dir) / "SOLVER_INFORMATIONS.DAT", SOLVER_COLUMNS)
    it = d.get("iterations", np.empty(0))
    if it.size == 0:
        return {"steps": 0, "unconverged_steps": None, "max_iterations": None,
                "mean_iterations": None, "steps_in_contact_phase": None,
                "unconverged_in_contact_phase": None}
    bad = it >= max_sweeps
    out = {"steps": int(it.size), "unconverged_steps": int(bad.sum()),
           "max_iterations": int(it.max()), "mean_iterations": float(it.mean()),
           "steps_in_contact_phase": None, "unconverged_in_contact_phase": None}
    if first_step is not None and 1 <= first_step <= it.size:
        tail = bad[first_step - 1:]
        out["steps_in_contact_phase"] = int(tail.size)
        out["unconverged_in_contact_phase"] = int(tail.sum())
        out["unconverged_before_contact"] = int(bad[:first_step - 1].sum())
    return out
